title: DKA Hospitalisations Have Jumped 24 Per Cent in Seven Years. Most Diabetics Had Never Heard of It.
excerpt: New data presented at ADA 2026 reveals diabetic ketoacidosis is driving nearly 60 per cent of all paediatric diabetes hospitalisations in the United States. The condition is now increasingly striking Type 2 patients — the demographic South Asians dominate globally.
body:
Diabetic ketoacidosis kills quietly and quickly. It develops when the body runs so low on insulin that it starts breaking down fat for energy, flooding the bloodstream with acids called ketones. Within hours, it can cause severe dehydration, organ failure, coma, and death. And according to multiple studies presented this week at the American Diabetes Association's 86th Scientific Sessions, it is being missed at a rate that should alarm every person living with diabetes.

The data, presented by Abbott on June 6, draws on analyses of over 340,000 patients across the United States. The findings are stark.

## The Numbers

Between 2017 and 2024, hospitalisations for diabetic ketoacidosis among Type 1 diabetes patients rose approximately 24 per cent, from 50 to 62 cases per 1,000 individuals. The increase was sharper among children than adults.

Among young people, DKA now accounts for nearly 60 per cent of all diabetes-related hospitalisations. Most require inpatient stays of up to a week, at costs reaching $38,000 per admission.

And here is the finding that should concern South Asians specifically: DKA is no longer just a Type 1 problem. A separate analysis of millions of insurance claims revealed that DKA is likely underreported in adults with Type 2 diabetes. When it is finally diagnosed — often only after admission — it is associated with longer hospital stays, higher costs, and increased mortality.

## Why Patients Miss It

DKA's early symptoms — nausea, fatigue, stomach pain, vomiting — mimic dozens of common illnesses. A study of over 100,000 patients found that emergency departments frequently fail to identify DKA at admission because the symptoms overlap with everything from food poisoning to the flu.

The definitive diagnosis requires blood tests for glucose, blood pH, bicarbonate levels, and ketones. These are not always ordered immediately. By the time they are, the condition may have progressed to a medical emergency.

Making matters worse, 64 per cent of diabetes patients do not test their ketone levels at all, according to a cross-sectional survey published in *BMJ Open Diabetes Research & Care*. Continuous glucose monitors, now used by over eight million people worldwide, do not measure ketones. A patient can have stable glucose readings and still be sliding into DKA.

## The South Asian Dimension

India has 101 million adults with Type 2 diabetes — the highest absolute number in the world. Across the diaspora, South Asians develop diabetes at younger ages and at lower BMIs than other ethnic groups. The ICMR-INDIAB study found that a large proportion of Indian diabetics are undiagnosed, unmonitored, and unaware of complications.

DKA awareness in South Asian communities is particularly low. Cultural factors — a tendency to attribute symptoms like fatigue and nausea to "acidity" or "heat" — delay medical attention. In rural India, where blood ketone testing infrastructure is virtually nonexistent, DKA often presents only when the patient is already in a coma.

For NRIs managing their diabetes in the United States, Canada, or the United Kingdom, the message is clearer: ketone monitoring should be routine, not reactive. The American Diabetes Association recommends testing ketones whenever blood glucose exceeds 240 mg/dL, during illness, or when experiencing unexplained nausea or abdominal pain.

## What Is Changing

Abbott has developed a dual glucose-ketone sensor — called Libre Duo — that combines continuous glucose and ketone monitoring in a single device. It received CE Mark in May 2026 and is pending FDA clearance in the United States. If approved, it could fundamentally change how diabetics detect rising ketone levels before they become life-threatening.

"DKA remains one of the most preventable emergencies in diabetes care," said Mahmood Kazemi, chief medical officer for Abbott's diabetes care division. "Too many people still miss early warning signs when ketone levels begin to rise."

For the 101 million diabetics in India and the estimated 30 million in the diaspora, that warning is overdue.
